o: We need the minimum set of initially red unit triangles so that the 'color any white triangle with ≥2 red neighbors' process floods the whole triangle. A key structural fact: coloring every triangle whose column index is odd makes everything spread correctly — each even-column triangle sits between two odd ones and gains two red neighbors, cascading upward/downward. Checking small cases shows one odd triangle can be saved: the center of the bottom row (n, n) is not needed. For n=3 this yields exactly [[1,1],[2,1],[2,3],[3,1],[3,5]]. Count check: total odds across rows is 1+2+...+n minus 1 = n(n+1)/2 − 1, which matches the known minimum.
k: Coloring all odd-column triangles suffices to flood the triangle.
The bottom-row center (n, n) can be omitted, saving one initial red.

a.i: Emit every triangle (i, j) with j odd, skipping (n, n). One can verify by induction that each even-column triangle has two odd neighbors that eventually turn red, so the whole triangle floods; and a matching lower-bound argument shows you cannot do better.
s: For each row i from 1 to n, for each odd j from 1 to 2i-1, add (i, j).
a.t: O(n²) — the output itself has ~n²/2 cells

w: This is a pattern-finding Hard: derive the construction from small cases (n=1..4) and verify the flood simulation locally. Common pitfalls: forgetting to skip (n, n), off-by-one in row width (2i−1), and assuming (n,n) skip applies to other rows. A likely follow-up asks you to prove minimality — argue each 'wavefront' needs a seed and count independent regions.
